timeline_eras.name: Asuka period (592–710)

capital.name: Asuka, Yamato
capital.description: Empress Suiko built her palaces in Asuka; Prince Shōtoku introduced the twelve cap ranks and the Seventeen-Article Constitution

timeline_eras.banner: The Taika Reforms — the ritsuryō state takes shape in Asuka

timeline_eras.name: Nara period (710–794)

capital.name: Heijō-kyō, Yamato
capital.description: The capital moved to Heijō-kyō in 710 and the Great Buddha of Tōdai-ji was consecrated — the high point of the ritsuryō state

timeline_eras.name: Heian period (794–1185)

capital.name: Heian-kyō, Yamashiro
capital.description: Emperor Kanmu moved the capital to Heian-kyō in 794; it stayed the imperial seat for over a thousand years

timeline_eras.banner: Cloistered rule and the rise of the samurai — on the eve of the Genpei War (c. 1180)

timeline_eras.name: Kamakura period (1185–1333)

capital.name: Kamakura, Sagami
capital.description: Minamoto no Yoritomo founded the first warrior government with Kamakura as its base

timeline_eras.banner: Warrior rule is born and the Kantō becomes the new political center

timeline_eras.name: Muromachi period (1336–1467)

capital.name: Muromachi, Kyoto (Flower Palace)
capital.description: Ashikaga Yoshimitsu built the "Flower Palace"; the Northern and Southern Courts were reunited in 1392

historic_battles.name: Battle of Okehazama (1560)

march_routes.desc: Set out from Kiyosu → prayed for victory at Atsuta Shrine → Zenshōji fort → charged into Okehazama
Marched west from Sunpu through Tōtōmi and Mikawa, camped at Kutsukake Castle, then advanced

historic_battles.brief: In 1560 Imagawa Yoshimoto led a huge army into Owari. Under cover of a sudden storm, Oda Nobunaga struck the Imagawa headquarters and killed Yoshimoto. The victory made Nobunaga's name; the Imagawa declined and Matsudaira Motoyasu (Ieyasu) broke free.

key_points.turning_point: Shielded by heavy rain, the Oda force fell on Yoshimoto's resting headquarters (accounts differ between a flanking surprise attack and a frontal assault).
key_points.forces: Oda c. 2,000–3,000; Imagawa c. 25,000, claimed 40,000 (figures vary).
key_points.aftermath: With Yoshimoto dead, Matsudaira Motoyasu left the Imagawa and in 1562 allied with Nobunaga (the Kiyosu Alliance); Nobunaga set out on his path to unify the realm.

narrator.name: Oda Nobunaga
narrator.title: "The Fool of Owari"
narrator.opening: Fifty years of human life, set against the heavens, are but a dream — all troops, hear me! Use this storm and take Yoshimoto's head!
narrator.tone: domineering and decisive, terse, with the wild edge of an all-or-nothing gamble

phases.title: Deployment
phases.desc: Imagawa Yoshimoto entered Owari with his main army and camped at Kutsukake Castle; his vanguard under Matsudaira Motoyasu ran supplies into the isolated Ōdaka Castle.
phases.line: Imagawa's horde has reached Kutsukake… and my retainers beg me to hole up in the castle? Hmph.

phases.title: Battle begins
phases.desc: The Imagawa took the Marune and Washizu forts. At dawn Nobunaga danced "Atsumori", rode out of Kiyosu with a handful of horsemen and gathered his men at Atsuta Shrine.
phases.line: Fifty years of human life… Bring my horse! Ride with me!

phases.title: Turning point
phases.desc: A sudden downpour let the Oda force close in unseen and strike the Imagawa headquarters resting on Okehazama-yama.
phases.line: Heaven is with me! Ride the storm straight at Yoshimoto's camp — one target only: his head!

phases.title: Outcome
phases.desc: Mōri Shinsuke struck down Imagawa Yoshimoto and the Imagawa army broke. Matsudaira Motoyasu returned to Okazaki and declared independence, later allying with Nobunaga.
phases.line: Yoshimoto is dead! …After today, the whole realm will know the name Oda of Owari.

debate.q: A surprise attack from the flank, or a frontal assault?
debate.a: The old story has Nobunaga circling round to fall on the Imagawa headquarters from behind; but the Shinchō kōki describes him charging straight at the Imagawa army, and Fujimoto Masayuki and others argue for a frontal attack. Both views still have supporters.

historic_battles.name: Fourth Battle of Kawanakajima (1561)

march_routes.desc: Left Kōfu for Kaizu Castle; a detachment raided Saijosan by night while the main army deployed at Hachimanbara
Left Kasugayama, camped on Saijosan by way of Zenkō-ji, saw through the plan and crossed the river by night

historic_battles.brief: In the fourth clash at Kawanakajima the Takeda split their army to raid Saijosan by night (the "woodpecker" tactic). Kenshin saw through it, slipped down the mountain overnight and fell on Shingen's headquarters out of the fog at Hachimanbara. Both sides suffered heavily and the result was a draw.

key_points.turning_point: Kenshin saw through the "woodpecker" plan and came down first; when the Takeda detachment returned the battle became a deadlock. The famous duel in which Kenshin rode alone into Shingen's camp is legend.
key_points.aftermath: Takeda Nobushige and Yamamoto Kansuke were killed; northern Shinano stayed largely under Takeda control and the rivalry went on to a fifth encounter.

narrator.name: Uesugi Kenshin
narrator.title: The Dragon of Echigo
narrator.opening: The fog is lifting — Shingen, your woodpecker pecked at an empty tree! Kuruma-gakari formation, follow me into Hachimanbara!
narrator.tone: lofty and righteous with an otherworldly air, terse and solemn; mark the duel and similar tales as legend

phases.title: Deployment
phases.desc: Kenshin camped on Saijosan with about 13,000 men, deep in Takeda territory, directly threatening Kaizu Castle.
phases.line: Here I sit on Saijosan — let us see how Shingen answers.

phases.title: Battle begins
phases.desc: Shingen adopted Yamamoto Kansuke's "woodpecker" plan: a detachment would raid Saijosan by night while the main army waited at Hachimanbara for the Uesugi to be driven down.
phases.line: More cooking smoke than usual over Kaizu… Shingen, you strike tonight, don't you?

phases.title: Turning point
phases.desc: Kenshin saw through the plan and quietly crossed the Chikuma River overnight. When the fog lifted, the Uesugi were already upon Shingen's headquarters, attacking in rotating waves.
phases.line: The fog has lifted — Shingen, I am right before your eyes!

phases.title: Outcome
phases.desc: The Takeda detachment returned and the Uesugi, caught front and rear, withdrew. Takeda Nobushige and Yamamoto Kansuke were killed; losses were heavy on both sides and the outcome was undecided.
phases.line: This battle settled nothing… but I have nothing to be ashamed of.

debate.q: Were the "woodpecker" plan and the duel of Shingen and Kenshin real?
debate.a: Both the "woodpecker" plan — a Takeda detachment circling behind Mount Saijo to drive the Uesugi down — and Kenshin riding into the Takeda camp to duel Shingen come from the Edo-period Kōyō gunkan; they are much disputed and may not be history.

historic_battles.name: Battle of Sekigahara (1600)

march_routes.desc: Ieyasu led the main army west along the Tōkaidō via Kiyosu to Akasaka in Mino
Hidetada took 30,000+ men along the Nakasendō, was held up at Ueda Castle by Sanada Masayuki and missed the battle
Mitsunari moved from Sawayama into Ōgaki Castle, then marched through the rainy night to deploy at Sekigahara
The western generals first took Fushimi Castle, then marched east to join Mitsunari

historic_battles.brief: After Toyotomi Hideyoshi's death, Tokugawa Ieyasu and Ishida Mitsunari came to blows. On the 15th day of the 9th month, 1600, they met at Sekigahara; Kobayakawa Hideaki and others defected from the West, and the East won within half a day. Ieyasu took the realm and founded the Edo shogunate three years later.

key_points.turning_point: Kobayakawa Hideaki turned on Ōtani Yoshitsugu's position and Wakisaka and three others followed in a chain of defections; the Mōri and Kikkawa never moved. Ieyasu's "prodding volley" at Matsuo-yama is one account.
key_points.forces: East c. 74,000–104,000; West over 80,000, though far fewer actually fought (figures vary).
key_points.aftermath: Mitsunari was executed and western daimyo were stripped or reduced; Ieyasu became shogun in 1603, and the Toyotomi fell at the Summer Siege of Osaka in 1615.

narrator.name: Tokugawa Ieyasu
narrator.title: Commander of the Eastern Army
narrator.opening: Today decides the realm. Is Kingo Chūnagon still sitting on the fence? — Pass the order: fire on Matsuo-yama and help him make up his mind!
narrator.tone: calm and patient with hidden impatience; the "prodding volley" is one account and should be marked so

phases.title: Deployment
phases.desc: While Ieyasu marched against the Uesugi, Mitsunari raised his army; the West took Fushimi Castle, while Hidetada's detachment on the Nakasendō was pinned at Ueda Castle by Sanada Masayuki.
phases.line: So Mitsunari has made his move… is Hidetada still tangled up with the Sanada?

phases.title: Battle begins
phases.desc: Ieyasu reached Akasaka in Mino; the western main force abandoned Ōgaki Castle, marched through the rainy night to Sekigahara and deployed around Sasao-yama.
phases.line: Mitsunari has left Ōgaki? Good — we settle it at Sekigahara.

phases.title: Turning point
phases.desc: The battle began once the morning fog lifted, and the West held the upper hand at first. At noon Kobayakawa Hideaki came down from Matsuo-yama against Ōtani Yoshitsugu, and Wakisaka and three others defected in turn.
phases.line: The banners on Matsuo-yama are moving… Kingo has finally made up his mind!

phases.title: Outcome
phases.desc: The West collapsed; Mitsunari fled, was captured and executed. Shimazu Yoshihiro broke out straight through the Eastern lines. The realm now belonged to Ieyasu.
phases.line: Decided in half a day. …The realm belongs, at last, to the Tokugawa.

debate.q: Did Ieyasu really fire on Matsuo hill to make Kobayakawa turn?
debate.a: The "prodding volley" — Ieyasu firing on Matsuo hill to force Kobayakawa Hideaki to declare himself — first appears, according to Goza Yūichi, in the war tale Keichō gunki of 1663, more than sixty years later. Some say Kobayakawa turned as soon as the fighting began and the volley was invented; Kasaya Kazuhiko and others disagree.

historic_battles.name: Battle of Dan-no-ura (1185)

march_routes.desc: After Yashima, Yoshitsune's fleet sailed west and gathered ships in Suō
Minamoto no Noriyori had already secured northern Kyūshū, cutting off the Taira retreat
Beaten at Ichi-no-Tani and Yashima, the Taira made a last stand from Hikoshima

historic_battles.brief: The final battle of the Genpei War. The Taira, holding Hikoshima, met Yoshitsune's fleet in the Kanmon Strait. When the battle turned, the Taira were crushed; the child Emperor Antoku went into the sea with his grandmother Nii-no-Ama, and the Taira clan was destroyed.

key_points.turning_point: In the afternoon the current turned and the Minamoto went on the offensive (the tidal explanation is the common view, though recently disputed); the Tale of the Heike says Yoshitsune ordered his men to shoot the enemy's oarsmen and helmsmen.
key_points.forces: Minamoto c. 840 ships, Taira c. 500 (per the Azuma Kagami and others; figures vary).
key_points.aftermath: The Taira were destroyed and the sacred sword sank into the sea; Minamoto no Yoritomo established warrior rule and the Kamakura period began.

narrator.name: Minamoto no Yoshitsune
narrator.title: The Minamoto's brilliant general
narrator.opening: The tide is about to turn! All hands — shoot the helmsmen and oarsmen on the Heike ships first! Today the Heike come to their end.
narrator.tone: young, bold and sharp, with a genius's pride and a touch of loneliness

phases.title: Deployment
phases.desc: Beaten at Yashima, the Taira held Hikoshima in Nagato; Minamoto no Noriyori already controlled northern Kyūshū, cutting off their retreat.
phases.line: The Heike have nowhere left to go — my brother Noriyori to the west, my fleet to the east.

phases.title: Battle begins
phases.desc: The fleets clashed in the Kanmon Strait. In the morning the current ran east, and the Taira, riding it, had the upper hand.
phases.line: The current is against us… hold on until it turns!

phases.title: Turning point
phases.desc: The current turned (the common view) and the Minamoto went on the attack; the Tale of the Heike says Yoshitsune had his men shoot the Taira oarsmen and helmsmen.
phases.line: The tide has turned! Shoot the helmsmen first — leave their ships dead in the water!

phases.title: Outcome
phases.desc: The Taira were routed. Nii-no-Ama leapt into the sea with the young Emperor Antoku, Taira no Tomomori followed, and the Taira clan was no more.
phases.line: …The end of the Heike. Yet the sacred sword lies at the bottom of the sea — what will my brother say?

debate.q: Did the tide decide the battle?
debate.a: Kuroita Katsumi argued that the current favoured the Taira in the morning and turned in the afternoon, carrying the Minamoto to victory. The maritime historian Kanazashi Shōzō later computed the tides for that day, found the current weak, and the theory has been questioned.

historic_battles.name: Satsuma Rebellion (1877)

factions.name: Government army
factions.leader: Yamagata Aritomo et al. (commander-in-chief Prince Arisugawa Taruhito)

march_routes.desc: Set out through the February snow, marched north via Hitoyoshi to besiege Kumamoto Castle, then sent troops north to block the relief force
The main government army came south from Fukuoka via Nankan and Takase toward Tabaruzaka
A rear force landed by sea near Yatsushiro and marched north to relieve Kumamoto Castle

historic_battles.brief: When the Meiji government abolished samurai privileges, disaffected Satsuma samurai rose under Saigō Takamori. Unable to take Kumamoto Castle, they fought government forces at Tabaruzaka for seventeen days and nights before falling back; Saigō died at Shiroyama, ending Japan's last civil war.

key_points.turning_point: Tani Tateki held Kumamoto Castle for over fifty days; in seventeen days of fighting at Tabaruzaka the government's numbers, supplies and modern rifles wore down the Satsuma army, and the rear landing left it attacked from both sides.
key_points.forces: Satsuma c. 20,000–30,000; government forces c. 80,000–100,000 (figures vary).
key_points.aftermath: Saigō took his own life at Shiroyama in Kagoshima on 24 September; armed samurai resistance ended and political struggle shifted to the Freedom and People's Rights Movement.

narrator.name: Saigō Takamori
narrator.title: Commander of the Satsuma army
narrator.opening: We go only to question the government… Kumamoto Castle is merely on our way — everyone, march north with me!
narrator.tone: generous and plain-spoken, deeply loyal, with an undertone of tragedy

phases.title: Deployment
phases.desc: Saigō Takamori led the Satsuma army out of Kagoshima through unusually heavy snow, heading north via Hitoyoshi toward Kumamoto Castle.
phases.line: We are only going to Tokyo to question the government — Kumamoto Castle is just on the way.

phases.title: Battle begins
phases.desc: Tani Tateki and the Kumamoto garrison held the castle; unable to storm it, the Satsuma army settled into a long siege.
phases.line: The Kumamoto garrison… so stubborn.

phases.title: Turning point
phases.desc: At Tabaruzaka the Satsuma army held off the government relief force for seventeen days and nights; the government broke through with superior numbers and supplies, sending in its sword-wielding Battōtai as well.
phases.line: The rain keeps falling, men and horses soaked… can we not get past Tabaruzaka?

phases.title: Outcome
phases.desc: The rear force landed near Yatsushiro and the siege of Kumamoto Castle was lifted on 14 April. The Satsuma army fell back south, and on 24 September Saigō took his own life at Shiroyama in Kagoshima.
phases.line: …Shin-don, this is far enough.

debate.a: In February 1877 the Private School faction seized Nakahara Hisao and other police officers sent home to Kagoshima and, under torture, extracted a "confession" that they had come to assassinate Saigō. The students were enraged and Saigō marched out soon after; whether he himself had meant to rise is disputed.

historic_battles.name: Battle of Ichi-no-Tani (1184)

factions.name: Minamoto
factions.leader: Minamoto no Noriyori, Minamoto no Yoshitsune
factions.strength: c. 74,000 riders (Azuma Kagami; the Gyokuyō diary says only one or two thousand)

factions.name: Taira
factions.leader: Taira no Tomomori, Taira no Shigehira

march_routes.desc: Minamoto no Noriyori led the main army out of Kyoto along the San’yō road and attacked the eastern Taira line at Ikuta Wood head-on
Minamoto no Yoshitsune took the rear army through Tanba, routed Taira no Sukemori at Mikusayama by night, then circled behind Ichi-no-Tani by way of Hiyodorigoe
The Taira crossed from Yashima in Sanuki, landed at Ōwada-no-tomari and occupied their old capital Fukuhara, holding a line from Ikuta Wood in the east to Ichi-no-Tani in the west

historic_battles.brief: In 1184 the Taira, recovered after fleeing the capital, occupied Fukuhara in Settsu and prepared to retake Kyoto. Minamoto no Yoritomo sent Noriyori and Yoshitsune west: Noriyori struck Ikuta Wood head-on while Yoshitsune circled through Tanba and fell on Ichi-no-Tani from behind. The Taira were routed; Tadanori, Atsumori and many others died, Shigehira was captured, and the rest withdrew by sea to Yashima.

key_points.turning_point: A detachment under Yoshitsune charged down the slopes behind Ichi-no-Tani (the "descent of Hiyodorigoe") and threw the western Taira position into chaos. Sources differ on where they came down and whether Yoshitsune led it himself.
key_points.forces: The Azuma Kagami gives Noriyori c. 54,000 riders and Yoshitsune c. 20,000; Kujō Kanezane’s diary Gyokuyō says the Taira had about 20,000 and the Minamoto only one or two thousand (figures vary).
key_points.aftermath: The Taira lost their foothold on Honshū and fell back to Yashima; the captive Shigehira was later sent to Kamakura. The next year (1185) the Minamoto won at Yashima and Dan-no-ura, and the Taira were destroyed.

narrator.name: Taira no Tomomori
narrator.title: Taira general
narrator.opening: Our main strength holds Ikuta Wood; let the Minamoto bring tens of thousands, they will not pass… but the hills behind Ichi-no-Tani in the west — is there truly no way down?
narrator.tone: calm and steadfast; sees the Taira decline yet fights on

phases.title: Deployment
phases.desc: The Taira fortified Fukuhara from Ikuta Wood in the east to Ichi-no-Tani in the west; Noriyori and Yoshitsune left Kyoto by two roads.
phases.line: Ikuta Wood to the east, Ichi-no-Tani to the west, mountains to the north — the Minamoto cannot break in here.

phases.title: Opening
phases.desc: Yoshitsune’s rear army marched west through Tanba and fell on Taira no Sukemori at Mikusayama by night; his force scattered.
phases.line: Sukemori routed at Mikusayama by a night attack? …So Yoshitsune is coming through the hills.

phases.title: Turning point
phases.desc: Noriyori’s main army pressed hard at Ikuta Wood while Yoshitsune’s band plunged down the cliffs behind Ichi-no-Tani; the western Taira camp burned and broke.
phases.line: Fire in the west? How can the enemy be behind us… they came down the mountain!

phases.title: Outcome
phases.desc: The Taira lines gave way one after another and men fought to reach the ships. Tomomori’s son Tomoakira died shielding his father; Tadanori, Atsumori and others fell and Shigehira was captured. The Taira withdrew to Yashima.
phases.line: Tomoakira held off the pursuers for me… and I took to the boat alone. Back to Yashima — we shall try again.

debate.q: Where was the famous descent of Hiyodorigoe?
debate.a: The sources never say exactly where Yoshitsune's men rode down the cliff. Hiyodorigoe is the usual answer, but it lies some way from Ichi-no-Tani; another reading is that Tada Yukitsuna took the Yumeno pass on the hill side while Yoshitsune himself went round behind Ichi-no-Tani.

historic_battles.name: Battle of Itsukushima (1555)

march_routes.desc: Sue Harukata led his army out of Suō, crossed in some 500 boats, landed on Itsukushima and besieged the Mōri fort of Miyao
Motonari came south from Yoshida-Kōriyama, crossed on a stormy night and landed at Tsutsumigaura on the island’s east shore
Kobayakawa Takakage brought the fleet round to land in front of Itsukushima Shrine

historic_battles.brief: In 1551 Sue Harukata overthrew his lord Ōuchi Yoshitaka (the Tainei-ji incident) and took control of the Ōuchi. After Mōri Motonari broke with him, Harukata crossed to Itsukushima in 1555 to take the Mōri fort there. Motonari crossed on a stormy night and struck; the Sue army collapsed and Harukata took his own life. The Mōri rose from here.

key_points.turning_point: At dawn on the 1st of the 10th month the main Mōri force charged down from Bakuchio behind the Sue camp while Kobayakawa’s men struck from the front; on the cramped island the larger army could not deploy and broke.
key_points.forces: Mōri 6,000 or more (one account); Sue traditionally over 20,000, though some recent work says under 10,000 (figures vary).
key_points.aftermath: Harukata fled to Ōenoura in the southwest of the island, found no boat and killed himself; Hironaka Takakane held out a few days before he fell. The Mōri then advanced into Suō and Nagato, and the Ōuchi were gone by 1557.

narrator.name: Mōri Motonari
narrator.title: the schemer of Aki
narrator.opening: Harukata has packed his whole army onto this little island… a high wind and heavy sea tonight — just right for a crossing.
narrator.tone: shrewd and patient, a master of stratagem and timing

phases.title: Deployment
phases.desc: Harukata’s army crossed to Itsukushima, camped on Tō-no-oka and besieged the Mōri fort of Miyao.
phases.line: “Take Miyao and Aki lies open” — that is what Harukata believes.

phases.title: Opening
phases.desc: In the storm Motonari put out from Jigozen with the main force, landed at Tsutsumigaura on the east shore and climbed Bakuchio; Kobayakawa Takakage’s fleet went round to the front.
phases.line: Every light out; row in silence. At first light we go down the hill.

phases.title: Turning point
phases.desc: The Mōri main body poured down from Bakuchio onto the Sue headquarters on Tō-no-oka while Kobayakawa attacked from the front; the Sue army fell into confusion in the narrow ground.
phases.line: Now! Here, on this island, their great numbers are only a burden.

phases.title: Outcome
phases.desc: Harukata fled southwest across the island, found no boat and killed himself at Ōenoura; Hironaka Takakane held a height for some days before he fell.
phases.line: Harukata is dead. …Next, Suō and Nagato.

debate.a: The Intoku taiheiki, the Yoshida monogatari and other accounts say Motonari built Miyao Castle in the spring of 1555 as bait to lure Sue Harukata onto the island. They were all written later, so whether it really was a ruse is hard to say.

historic_battles.name: Battle of Nagashino (1575)

march_routes.desc: Nobunaga marched from Gifu with some 30,000, joined Ieyasu at Okazaki and dug in on the west bank of the Rengo stream at Shitaragahara behind horse-stopping fences
Ieyasu’s Tokugawa troops took the forward position on Takamatsu hill
Katsuyori marched from Kai through Shinano into Mikawa and besieged the Tokugawa castle of Nagashino
Leaving men to hold the siege, Katsuyori crossed the Takizawa river and faced the allies at Shitaragahara
Sakai Tadatsugu took a flying column round by night to storm the Takeda fort on Tobigasuyama watching Nagashino

historic_battles.brief: In 1575 Takeda Katsuyori invaded Mikawa and besieged Nagashino. Oda Nobunaga came with a large army and, with Tokugawa Ieyasu, entrenched behind fences at Shitaragahara. On the 21st of the 5th month the Takeda attacked the fenced line head-on and suffered terribly under massed gunfire; Yamagata Masakage, Baba Nobuharu and many senior retainers died.

key_points.turning_point: At dawn Sakai Tadatsugu’s column took the Tobigasuyama fort, threatening the Takeda rear; the main army attacked the fences at Shitaragahara and met the allies’ massed guns (the famous "three-rank volley" is now widely doubted).
key_points.forces: Oda–Tokugawa c. 38,000 and Takeda c. 15,000 by the common view (figures vary).
key_points.aftermath: The Takeda lost a generation of senior retainers and could no longer push west; in 1582 Oda and Tokugawa invaded Kai and the Takeda fell.

narrator.name: Takeda Katsuyori
narrator.title: head of the Takeda of Kai
narrator.opening: Tobigasuyama is lost… there is no way back, so forward! Can the Oda behind their fences stop the best of the Takeda?
narrator.tone: proud and combative, carrying his father Shingen’s name; restless and unwilling to yield

phases.title: Deployment
phases.desc: The Takeda besieged Nagashino, held by Okudaira Sadamasa with about 500 men; Torii Suneemon slipped out to fetch help.
phases.line: Nagashino has only five hundred men. Take it and Mikawa lies open.

phases.title: Opening
phases.desc: The allies reached Shitaragahara and built fences along the Rengo stream; Katsuyori left a siege force and advanced to face them. That night Sakai Tadatsugu’s column set off round toward Tobigasuyama.
phases.line: The Oda hide behind fences and will not come out? …Then we break them head-on.

phases.title: Turning point
phases.desc: Tobigasuyama fell; wave after wave of Takeda troops charged the fences and were cut down by gunfire.
phases.line: One company falls, the next goes in… why do the fences still stand!

phases.title: Outcome
phases.desc: The Takeda broke. Yamagata Masakage, Baba Nobuharu, Naitō Masahide and other senior retainers were killed; Katsuyori escaped to Kai with a handful of men.
phases.line: My father’s old retainers… all of them lie on this field.

debate.q: Three thousand guns firing in three ranks — true?
debate.a: The Shinchō kōki only says five gun commanders were put in charge; it says nothing of firing in three ranks. "Three thousand guns in three ranks" comes from the Edo-period Hoan Shinchōki and spread once Meiji textbooks taught it as fact.

historic_battles.name: Battle of Yamazaki (1582)

march_routes.desc: Hearing of Honnō-ji, Hideyoshi made peace with the Mōri and raced back east from Bitchū (the "Great Return from Chūgoku") via Himeji and Amagasaki, joining Oda Nobutaka and Niwa Nagahide at Tonda in Settsu
After killing Nobunaga at Honnō-ji, Mitsuhide failed to win over the Hosokawa and Tsutsui and drew up behind the Enmyōji stream by Shōryūji Castle

historic_battles.brief: On the 2nd of the 6th month, 1582, Akechi Mitsuhide killed Oda Nobunaga at Honnō-ji. Hashiba Hideyoshi, besieging Takamatsu in Bitchū, quickly made peace with the Mōri, hurried back east and met the Akechi army at Yamazaki on the 13th. The Akechi were beaten and Mitsuhide died at Ogurusu while fleeing toward Sakamoto.

key_points.turning_point: The armies faced each other across the Enmyōji stream and fighting began late in the afternoon. Ikeda Tsuneoki and others crossed on the right and struck the flank; the Akechi line gave way. (Later tradition made the struggle for Mount Tennō the decisive moment, and "Tennōzan" became a byword for a showdown.)
key_points.aftermath: After Mitsuhide’s death Hideyoshi steered the Oda succession at the Kiyosu conference, beat Shibata Katsuie at Shizugatake the next year and set out to unify the realm.

narrator.name: Hashiba Hideyoshi
narrator.title: leader of the Great Return
narrator.opening: Our lord murdered at Honnō-ji… Mitsuhide, did you think the Mōri still had me pinned in Bitchū? March day and night — back to Kyoto!
narrator.tone: quick and decisive, a born winner of hearts; warm in tone with an edge

phases.title: Deployment
phases.desc: Nobunaga died at Honnō-ji. Mitsuhide sought allies while Hideyoshi, far off in Bitchū, made peace with the Mōri the moment he heard.
phases.line: Sign the peace at once! Takamatsu is finished business.

phases.title: Opening
phases.desc: Hideyoshi hurried east through Himeji and Amagasaki and joined Oda Nobutaka and Niwa Nagahide at Tonda. Tsutsui Junkei never came to Mitsuhide’s aid; the Akechi drew up around Shōryūji Castle.
phases.line: Gentlemen, the hour to avenge our lord has come!

phases.title: Turning point
phases.desc: The armies faced each other across the Enmyōji stream and clashed toward evening. Ikeda Tsuneoki crossed on the right and fell on the Akechi flank, which collapsed; the whole line fell back.
phases.line: Our right is across! The Akechi line is wavering — everyone forward!

phases.title: Outcome
phases.desc: Mitsuhide fell back into Shōryūji Castle and slipped out at night for Sakamoto, but was killed by villagers hunting fugitives at Ogurusu (some say he took his own life after being wounded).
phases.line: Mitsuhide is dead. …Now — who will inherit the Oda realm?

debate.q: Was it really the race for Mount Tennō that decided it?
debate.a: "Whoever held Mount Tennō won" comes mainly from later books such as the Taikōki; the fighting itself began at the foot of the mountain and along the Enmyōji stream. The phrase "Tennōzan" for a decisive moment grew from that story.

historic_battles.name: Battle of Toba–Fushimi (1868)

factions.name: New government army
factions.leader: Saigō Takamori and others (mainly Satsuma and Chōshū)

factions.name: Former shogunate army
factions.leader: Ōkōchi Masatada and others (Aizu and Kuwana troops, the Shinsengumi)

march_routes.desc: The main former-shogunate force marched north from Osaka "to punish Satsuma", heading for Kyoto along the Toba road
Aizu troops and the Shinsengumi occupied the Fushimi magistrate’s office
Satsuma troops came south from Tō-ji to block the road at Koeda bridge in Toba
Satsuma and Chōshū troops took position around Gokōnomiya, their guns trained on the magistrate’s office

historic_battles.brief: After the return of power to the throne and the restoration of imperial rule in 1867, the quarrel between Satsuma and the former shogunate came to a head. On the 3rd of the 1st month, 1868, shogunate troops marching on Kyoto clashed at Toba and Fushimi with a smaller new-government force led by Satsuma and Chōshū, and lost. Tokugawa Yoshinobu fled Osaka Castle by ship for Edo. The Boshin War had begun.

key_points.turning_point: The new government raised the imperial brocade banner, making the shogunate side "enemies of the court"; the retreating troops were refused entry to Yodo Castle, then the Tsu domain changed sides at Yamazaki and shelled them, and the whole army gave way.
key_points.forces: Former shogunate c. 15,000; new government c. 5,000.
key_points.aftermath: On the night of the 6th Yoshinobu quietly left Osaka Castle and sailed for Edo in the Kaiyō Maru, where he submitted. Edo Castle was handed over in the 4th month and the war moved to the northeast and Hakodate.

narrator.name: Hijikata Toshizō
narrator.title: vice-commander of the Shinsengumi
narrator.opening: Commander Kondō has a bullet wound, so Fushimi is mine to command. Satsuma’s guns sit on the Gokōnomiya rise — the Shinsengumi do not fall back.
narrator.tone: cold and resolute; quick to grasp what modern guns had changed

phases.title: Deployment
phases.desc: The shogunate army marched north from Osaka; Satsuma men blocked the road at Koeda bridge in Toba, and Satsuma and Chōshū troops held the Gokōnomiya rise in Fushimi.
phases.line: Get past this road and Kyoto is right in front of us.

phases.title: Opening
phases.desc: At Koeda bridge the shogunate column demanded passage; talks failed, Satsuma’s guns opened fire and fighting broke out at Toba and Fushimi at once. The Fushimi magistrate’s office was shelled and set ablaze.
phases.line: Guns at Toba! …The office is on fire — out, and charge!

phases.title: Turning point
phases.desc: The new government raised the brocade banner; the shogunate troops were pushed back around Senryōmatsu and, trying to fall back into Yodo Castle, found its gates shut against them.
phases.line: The brocade banner… so now we are the court’s enemies? Swords and spears are no match for their guns.

phases.title: Outcome
phases.desc: The Tsu domain turned on them at Yamazaki and shelled them from across the river; the army fell back to Osaka. That night Tokugawa Yoshinobu quietly left Osaka Castle and sailed for Edo in the Kaiyō Maru.
phases.line: The shogun is gone… but the war is not over. On to Edo, and then north.

debate.q: Why did Yoshinobu leave his army and sail for Edo?
debate.a: Late in life Yoshinobu explained in the Sekimukai hikki that he would not bear the name of "enemy of the court" and decided to return east first and think again. Opinions of what he did differed widely, then and since.

historic_battles.name: Battle of Anegawa (1570)

march_routes.desc: Nobunaga marched from Gifu into northern Ōmi, burned the town below Odani Castle, besieged Yokoyama Castle and camped at Tatsugahana, where Tokugawa Ieyasu joined him
Asakura Kagetake arrived with about 8,000 men and camped on Ōyoriyama east of Odani Castle, joining Azai Nagamasa’s 5,000
Before dawn on the 28th the Azai and Asakura split in two and formed up at Nomura and Mitamura on the north bank of the Ane

historic_battles.brief: In 1570 Azai Nagamasa broke with Nobunaga and came to the aid of the Asakura, forcing Nobunaga to retreat from Echizen. That summer Nobunaga and Tokugawa Ieyasu invaded northern Ōmi and met the Azai–Asakura army on the banks of the Ane. Hard pressed at first, the Oda side won after the Tokugawa struck the enemy flank — but Odani Castle, the Azai seat, held out.

key_points.turning_point: The Oda line was in danger for a while; Ieyasu saw that the Azai–Asakura front was stretched thin and sent Sakakibara Yasumasa against its flank. The Asakura broke first, then the Azai.
key_points.forces: Azai about 5,000 and Asakura about 8,000, some 13,000 in all; the article gives no figure for the Oda–Tokugawa side.
key_points.aftermath: The Oda side took over 1,100 heads and the Azai lost senior men such as Endō Naotsune; Yokoyama Castle soon surrendered and Kinoshita Hideyoshi was put in charge of it, but Odani stayed in Azai hands.

narrator.name: Azai Nagamasa
narrator.title: lord of northern Ōmi
narrator.opening: It was I who broke faith with Nobunaga first… so be it — let it be settled at the Ane.
narrator.tone: upright, carrying both his betrayal of his brother-in-law Nobunaga and his loyalty to the Asakura

phases.title: Deployment
phases.desc: Nobunaga burned the town below Odani, besieged Yokoyama Castle and camped with Ieyasu at Tatsugahana; the Asakura relief force reached Ōyoriyama, bringing the allies to about 13,000.
phases.line: They have burned the town below Odani… but the Asakura have come — they are on Ōyoriyama.

phases.title: Opening
phases.desc: The Azai and Asakura broke camp on the 27th, only to reappear before dawn on the 28th on the north bank, at Nomura and Mitamura. The Tokugawa went for the Asakura at Mitamura in the west, Nobunaga’s guard and the three Western Mino lords for the Azai at Nomura in the east; fighting began around six.
phases.line: Breaking camp yesterday was for their eyes only. Across the Ane!

phases.title: Turning point
phases.desc: The Oda were hard pressed; Ieyasu, seeing the enemy line overstretched, sent Sakakibara Yasumasa at its flank. The Asakura gave way first, then the Azai.
phases.line: The Asakura line broken from the side? …Where did the Tokugawa come from!

phases.title: Outcome
phases.desc: The Oda side took over 1,100 heads. Nobunaga chased the Azai to the foot of Odani, judged it too strong to storm and fell back to Yokoyama, which soon surrendered and was given to Kinoshita Hideyoshi. The Azai lost Endō Naotsune and other senior men.
phases.line: Endō Naotsune is dead too… back to Odani — we hold the mountain castle.

debate.q: A pitched battle, or a surprise attack by the Azai and Asakura?
debate.a: The usual view is that the armies formed up across the Ane and fought head-on. Takazawa Hitoshi, reading the Shinchō kōki line that the enemy "seemed to have broken camp, yet before dawn on the 28th came within thirty chō", argues for a surprise attack that caught the Oda before they could form up.

historic_battles.name: Battle of Mikatagahara (1573)

factions.name: Takeda
factions.strength: c. 27,000 (the most the Takeda could field)

factions.name: Tokugawa–Oda
factions.strength: Tokugawa c. 8,000, plus an Oda relief force (figures vary; one says c. 3,000)

march_routes.desc: Shingen left Kōfu on the 3rd of the 10th month 1572, entered Tōtōmi by way of Shinano and besieged Futamata Castle
On the 22nd of the 12th month the Takeda left Futamata westwards, passed by Hamamatsu Castle and made for the Mikatagahara plateau
Overruling some of his retainers, Ieyasu led the allies out of Hamamatsu to catch the Takeda from behind as they went down the Iwaita slope

historic_battles.brief: In 1572 Takeda Shingen launched his westward campaign into Tōtōmi. At the end of the year his army marched past Tokugawa Ieyasu’s Hamamatsu Castle towards Mikatagahara; Ieyasu came out after it, only to be routed by a Takeda army already drawn up for battle, and barely escaped back to his castle.

key_points.turning_point: The Takeda seemed to be bypassing Hamamatsu, drawing Ieyasu out to fight in the open; when he reached Mikatagahara the Takeda were waiting in fish-scale formation.
key_points.forces: The Takeda brought about 27,000, the most they ever fielded; the Tokugawa could raise only about 8,000, plus the Oda relief force (numbers vary).
key_points.aftermath: One account gives about 200 Takeda casualties against about 2,000 Tokugawa; Natsume Yoshinobu and others died covering Ieyasu’s escape. The Takeda wintered in Tōtōmi and took Noda Castle the next year, but Shingen fell ill and died on the way home.

narrator.name: Tokugawa Ieyasu
narrator.title: lord of Hamamatsu
narrator.opening: The strongest army in the land is marching across my domain… am I just to watch?
narrator.tone: young and proud, unwilling to look weak; learns patience from defeat

phases.title: The march west
phases.desc: Shingen left Kōfu on the 3rd of the 10th month, entered Tōtōmi via Shinano and besieged Futamata; the castle surrendered on the 19th of the 12th month, and northern Tōtōmi became Takeda land.
phases.line: Futamata has fallen too… Shingen will come for Hamamatsu next.

phases.title: The sortie
phases.desc: The Takeda left Futamata heading west but marched straight past Hamamatsu, as if bound for the Mikatagahara plateau; against some of his retainers’ advice Ieyasu led the allies out in pursuit.
phases.line: Marching right past my gate? To be scorned like this — what kind of warrior would stand for it? Out!

phases.title: Battle
phases.desc: On the plateau the Takeda were already waiting in fish-scale formation; Ieyasu spread his men in crane’s-wing order, and in about two hours before sunset the allies were broken. Natsume Yoshinobu and others died so that Ieyasu could escape.
phases.line: They were waiting for us all along… it was a trap!

phases.title: Outcome
phases.desc: Ieyasu got back to Hamamatsu with a handful of men and, the story goes, threw open the gates and lit fires (the "empty fort ploy"); the night raid at Saigagake appears only in later Tokugawa sources. The Takeda wintered in Tōtōmi and took Noda Castle the next year, but Shingen fell ill and died on the way home.
phases.line: Natsume died in my place… this life of mine was given back to me.

debate.q: Where exactly was the battle fought?
debate.a: Nobody knows for sure. There is a memorial stone near the Mikatahara cemetery, but the site is not established. Hirayama Yū lists four main theories — Azukimochi, Nearai (above the Iwaita slope), Ōshibahara and Ōya; few sources describe the field directly, and some sites have been moved or lost to development.

historic_battles.name: Battle of Minatogawa (1336)

factions.name: Ashikaga
factions.strength: est. c. 35,000 (the Taiheiki says over 500,000; figures vary)

factions.name: Nitta–Kusunoki
factions.strength: est. c. 17,500 (the Taiheiki says over 50,000; figures vary)

march_routes.desc: After winning Kyūshū at Tatarahama, Takauji came east by way of Tomo in Bingo, joined the Hosokawa fleets from Shikoku and advanced by sea
Ashikaga Tadayoshi led the main land army east along the Saigoku road
Nitta Yoshisada, bogged down besieging the Akamatsu in Harima, fell back to Hyōgo on the 13th to regroup
His plan rejected, Kusunoki Masashige was ordered to Hyōgo on the 16th and joined Yoshisada on the 24th

historic_battles.brief: In 1336 Ashikaga Takauji, who had been driven to Kyūshū, rebuilt his strength and came back east by land and sea. Emperor Go-Daigo sent Nitta Yoshisada and Kusunoki Masashige to stop him at Hyōgo in Settsu. An outflanking landing by the Ashikaga fleet cut Nitta off from Kusunoki, and Masashige fought on alone until he took his own life.

key_points.turning_point: The Hosokawa fleet moved east as if to land there, drawing Yoshisada after it; the ships at the rear turned and landed at Wada Point, cutting the Nitta off from the Kusunoki.
key_points.forces: The Taiheiki claims over 500,000 Ashikaga against over 50,000 imperial troops; later estimates put it at about 35,000 to 17,500. Masashige himself had only some 700 riders.
key_points.aftermath: When Hosokawa Jōzen landed at Ikuta Wood, Yoshisada fell back east for fear of being cut off; left alone, Masashige charged Tadayoshi’s army and in the end took his life together with his brother Masasue.

narrator.name: Kusunoki Masashige
narrator.title: Go-Daigo’s loyal commander
narrator.opening: Let the Ashikaga into the capital and crush them between us — the court would not hear of it. Then at Hyōgo I shall do my duty.
narrator.tone: clear-eyed and calm, loyal to the end though he sees the odds

phases.title: The march east
phases.desc: Takauji came by sea and Tadayoshi by land; Nitta Yoshisada fell back to Hyōgo, and Masashige, sent down from the capital, joined him on the 24th.
phases.line: By land and sea — what a host… Lord Nitta, let us drink together tonight.

phases.title: Deployment
phases.desc: Yoshisada held Wada Point with 25,000 and Wakiya Yoshisuke the Kyōjima island; Masashige, with only some 700 riders, took the hill of Egeyama against the enemy coming by land.
phases.line: I have but seven hundred riders and no one else’s men — the Kusunoki will hold this hill.

phases.title: Turning point
phases.desc: The Hosokawa fleet sailed east to feint a landing and drew Yoshisada after it; the rear ships turned and landed at Wada Point, splitting the Nitta from the Kusunoki. When Hosokawa Jōzen came ashore at Ikuta Wood, Yoshisada withdrew east rather than be cut off.
phases.line: Lord Nitta has gone east… we are cut off — the enemy before us and behind.

phases.title: Outcome
phases.desc: Masashige led his 700 riders against Tadayoshi’s great army and broke through again and again, until at last he and his brother Masasue took their own lives.
phases.line: Break the enemy ahead, then turn on the one behind… Masasue, this is as far as we go.

debate.q: Why did Nitta Yoshisada deploy with his back to the sea?
debate.a: Yoshisada camped on Wada Point, with sea on three sides and his back to the Ashikaga fleet; if Kusunoki and Wakiya to the north were broken he would be surrounded with nowhere to go — a "strange deployment", as it has long been called. Some suggest he chose a "back to the water" position on purpose, so that his men would fight to the death.

historic_battles.name: Battle of Shizugatake (1583)

march_routes.desc: Before the snows had gone, Katsuie led some 30,000 out of Kitanoshō in Echizen and took up position at Yanagase in Ōmi on the 12th of the 3rd month
Hideyoshi camped at Kinomoto with about 50,000 on the 19th; both sides fortified the hills
With Hideyoshi away, Sakuma Morimasa slipped round Lake Yogo to strike the Ōiwayama fort
The "great Mino return": leaving Ōgaki at 2 p.m., Hideyoshi covered 13 ri (about 52 km) back to Kinomoto in five hours

historic_battles.brief: After the Honnō-ji incident of 1582, Hashiba Hideyoshi and Shibata Katsuie fought over control of the Oda house. In the 4th month of 1583 their armies faced each other around Shizugatake in Ōmi. Katsuie’s general Sakuma Morimasa won a surprise attack but would not pull back; Hideyoshi raced back from Mino to counter-attack, Maeda Toshiie left the field, and Katsuie, routed, withdrew to Kitanoshō and took his own life.

key_points.turning_point: Hearing at Ōgaki that Ōiwayama had fallen, Hideyoshi marched 52 km in five hours (the "great Mino return"), while Niwa Nagahide crossed Lake Biwa and secured the Shizugatake fort.
key_points.forces: Hideyoshi with about 50,000 (as reported) against Katsuie’s 30,000 or so.
key_points.aftermath: Most of the old Oda retainers came over to Hideyoshi, who soon began building Osaka Castle on the site of the Ishiyama Hongan-ji — his first step to ruling the realm.

narrator.name: Shibata Katsuie
narrator.title: senior elder of the Oda house
narrator.opening: The moment the snow melted I marched. I will not hand Lord Nobunaga’s realm to that monkey.
narrator.tone: a fierce old soldier, no schemer

phases.title: Standoff
phases.desc: Katsuie reached Yanagase with some 30,000 on the 12th; Hideyoshi camped at Kinomoto with about 50,000 on the 19th. Both sides dug in on the hills and neither moved first.
phases.line: The monkey is building forts at Kinomoto… very well, we shall see who loses patience first.

phases.title: Surprise attack
phases.desc: Oda Nobutaka rose again at Gifu and Hideyoshi went to Mino, entering Ōgaki Castle. Katsuie seized the moment and sent Sakuma Morimasa against the Ōiwayama fort; Nakagawa Kiyohide was killed. But Morimasa ignored the order to fall back and stayed forward.
phases.line: Ōiwayama is ours! Morimasa, that is enough — come back! …He will not listen.

phases.title: Turning point
phases.desc: Niwa Nagahide crossed Lake Biwa and held the Shizugatake fort; Hideyoshi, told at Ōgaki, set out at 2 p.m. and was back at Kinomoto five hours later. At dawn the Hashiba army attacked, the "Seven Spears of Shizugatake" among them.
phases.line: Was the monkey not in Mino? …All those torches overnight — he is back!

phases.title: Outcome
phases.desc: In the thick of it Maeda Toshiie suddenly withdrew from the line and the Shibata army’s spirit broke. Katsuie fell back to Kitanoshō, was surrounded on the 23rd and on the 24th took his life with his wife Oichi.
phases.line: Toshiie too… back to Kitanoshō. Oichi — forgive me, for all of it.

debate.q: Why did Maeda Toshiie leave the field?
debate.a: At the height of the fighting Maeda Toshiie, posted on Shigeyama, suddenly pulled out, and the Shibata army collapsed. It is usually supposed that he had long since accepted Hideyoshi’s overtures — but how far he had agreed in advance, and when he decided to go, is not established.

historic_battles.name: Battle of Komaki–Nagakute (1584)

march_routes.desc: Ikeda Tsuneoki seized Inuyama; Hideyoshi arrived there on the 27th and camped at Gakuden
Ieyasu hurried from Kiyosu to Komakiyama Castle and ringed it with forts and earthworks
The "drive into Mikawa": four columns under Ikeda Tsuneoki, Mori Nagayoshi, Hori Hidemasa and Hashiba Hidetsugu swung towards Mikawa, taking Iwasaki Castle on the way
Ieyasu found out, left Komaki by night for Obata Castle and came up behind the raiding columns

historic_battles.brief: In 1584 Oda Nobukatsu and Tokugawa Ieyasu joined against Hashiba Hideyoshi and the armies faced each other around Komaki in Owari. Hideyoshi sent a raiding force into Mikawa; Ieyasu caught it at Nagakute, where Ikeda Tsuneoki and Mori Nagayoshi were killed. But Hideyoshi then made a separate peace with Nobukatsu, and Ieyasu had to stop too.

key_points.turning_point: Ieyasu saw through the raid and followed it by night; Hashiba Hidetsugu was routed at Hakusanbayashi, and at Nagakute Mori Nagayoshi was shot and Ikeda Tsuneoki killed by Nagai Naokatsu.
key_points.aftermath: Some 2,500 Hashiba men died at Nagakute against 590 on the other side; on the 12th of the 11th month Hideyoshi made peace with Nobukatsu, and Ieyasu came to terms too, sending his son Ogimaru (Yūki Hideyasu) to Osaka as Hideyoshi’s adopted son.

narrator.name: Hashiba Hideyoshi
narrator.title: Nobunaga’s successor
narrator.opening: Lord Nobukatsu has sided with Ieyasu… fine. Let us see what the old fox of the Tōkaidō can do.
narrator.tone: shrewd and easy-going; if he cannot win one way he wins another

phases.title: Standoff
phases.desc: On the 13th Ikeda Tsuneoki went over to Hideyoshi and seized Inuyama; on the 17th Sakai Tadatsugu and others beat Mori Nagayoshi at Haguro. Ieyasu held Komakiyama, Hideyoshi camped at Gakuden, both dug forts, and the war stalled.
phases.line: Ieyasu is dug in on Komaki behind fort after fort… at this rate neither of us can move.

phases.title: The raid
phases.desc: Ikeda Tsuneoki proposed striking Mikawa while it lay empty, so Ieyasu could not stay at Komaki. Hideyoshi agreed and four columns set out; at dawn on the 9th they took Iwasaki Castle.
phases.line: Tsuneoki wants to raid Mikawa… very well, let them go.

phases.title: Nagakute
phases.desc: Ieyasu slipped out of Komaki by night to Obata Castle; at dawn his men fell on Hashiba Hidetsugu at Hakusanbayashi and routed him. Around ten the main armies clashed at Nagakute for two hours; Mori Nagayoshi was shot dead and Ikeda Tsuneoki killed by Nagai Naokatsu.
phases.line: Hidetsugu beaten? Tsuneoki and Nagayoshi both dead… Ieyasu came up behind them.

phases.title: Peace
phases.desc: Some 2,500 Hashiba men died at Nagakute against 590 Oda–Tokugawa; after that the front stood still. On the 12th of the 11th month Hideyoshi made a separate peace with Nobukatsu, and Ieyasu stopped too, sending his son Ogimaru (Yūki Hideyasu) to Osaka as Hideyoshi’s adopted son.
phases.line: I lost a battle, but Lord Nobukatsu came to make peace first. Ieyasu, you have no cause left to fight.

debate.a: In the field at Nagakute the Tokugawa side won handsomely, killing Ikeda Tsuneoki and Mori Nagayoshi; but Hideyoshi held Mino, Ise and elsewhere and got Nobukatsu to make a separate peace, leaving Ieyasu with no cause to fight. Hence the usual verdict: a tactical win for Oda–Tokugawa, a strategic win for Hashiba.

historic_battles.name: Summer Siege of Osaka (1615)

factions.name: Toyotomi
factions.leader: Toyotomi Hideyori (with Sanada Nobushige, Mōri Yoshimasa and others)

march_routes.desc: A shogunate column of about 35,000 came by the Yamato road towards Osaka
Ieyasu and Hidetada brought the main army south to deploy before Tennōji and Okayama
Gotō Masachika, Sanada Nobushige and others marched out to meet the shogunate army on the Yamato road
On the 7th the Toyotomi army drew up at Tennōji (Sanada, Mōri and others) and Okayama

historic_battles.brief: After the peace that ended the winter siege of 1614, Osaka Castle’s outer moat and even its second and third baileys were filled in. War broke out again in 1615, and the Toyotomi, their defences gone, came out to fight: Gotō Masachika fell at Dōmyōji on the 6th of the 5th month, Sanada Nobushige and others died fighting at Tennōji–Okayama on the 7th, and on the 8th the castle fell. Toyotomi Hideyori and his mother Yodo-dono took their own lives, and the Toyotomi line came to an end.

key_points.turning_point: With the moats filled the castle could not be held, so the Toyotomi had to fight in the open — and, poorly coordinated, they were beaten piecemeal at Dōmyōji.
key_points.forces: In the summer campaign the shogunate had about 165,000, the Toyotomi about 55,000.
key_points.aftermath: On the 8th Hideyori, Yodo-dono and others killed themselves in a surviving storehouse in the Yamazato bailey, ending the Toyotomi; no daimyo was left who could stand against the Tokugawa.

narrator.name: Sanada Nobushige
narrator.title: rōnin commander at Osaka
narrator.opening: They have filled in the moats… this castle can no longer be held. If we are to win, we must go out and fight.
narrator.tone: cool and decisive; knows the cause is lost but means to be remembered

phases.title: After the winter siege
phases.desc: After the winter peace the outer moat and the second and third baileys were filled in; in the 3rd month of 1615 the Kyoto deputy reported unrest among the rōnin in Osaka, and war came again.
phases.line: The moats are gone… to win, we must fight outside the walls.

phases.title: Dōmyōji
phases.desc: At Dōmyōji–Konda, Gotō Masachika (Matabei) reached Komatsuyama first and fought more than twenty thousand under Date Masamune and others on his own until he fell; Sanada and the rest arrived later and fought the Date.
phases.line: Matabei is already… we came too late.

phases.title: Tennōji–Okayama
phases.desc: The Toyotomi drew up at Tennōji (Sanada Nobushige, Mōri Yoshimasa and others, about 14,500) and Okayama; the Sanada charged Ieyasu’s headquarters, and after bitter fighting Nobushige was killed and the Toyotomi fell back.
phases.line: One target only — Ieyasu’s own camp!

phases.title: The fall
phases.desc: Osaka Castle fell; Hideyori, Yodo-dono, Ōno Harunaga and others killed themselves in a surviving storehouse in the Yamazato bailey, and the Toyotomi were no more.
phases.line: …Lord Hideyori, Nobushige goes ahead of you.

debate.q: Was filling in the inner moats a trick by Ieyasu?
debate.a: The popular story is that the peace covered only the outer moat and the Tokugawa treacherously filled the inner ones too. But the daimyo’s letters from the time show no sign of a quarrel over the work, and some research holds that filling the second and third baileys as well as the outer moat was agreed from the start, and accepted by the Osaka side.
